steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that studies how well instruction fine-tuned LLMs do zero-shot classification on social media / computational social science tasks, and whether more complex prompts actually help.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - instruction fine-tuning -> LLMs transfer to unseen tasks at scale
  - immediate effort to measure zero-shot performance on challenging tasks
  - social media analysis: complex, domain-specific tasks; harm reduction, stopping misinformation
  - LLMs could help CSS tasks: automatic data annotation + social media analysis
  - need to understand capabilities/limitations of latest instruction-tuned LLMs
- Research questions
  - RQ1: zero-shot performance on social media classification; vs smaller SOTA fine-tuned models
  - RQ2: most effective prompt strategies, zero-shot
  - RQ3: data leakage - were datasets already in pre-training corpus?
- Setup
  - controlled experiments, two off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLMs, different prompting strategies
  - GPT-3.5-turbo (GPT): most widely used proprietary model
  - OpenAssistant-LLaMA (LLaMA-OA): open source, instruction-tuned on LLaMA
  - six social media analysis NLP tasks
  - prompt complexity levels: few-shot examples, publication info of benchmark datasets
  - baselines: standard techniques e.g. fine-tuning BERT
- Scope
  - off-the-shelf instruction-tuned models, social media classification, zero-shot
  - foundation models without instruction tuning: out of scope
- Findings
  - (i) task-specific fine-tuned models generally beat LLMs in most zero-shot settings, even when much smaller (e.g. BERT-large)
  - (ii) prompting ensembles (e.g. on synonyms) improve performance and robustness
  - (iii) detailed/complex prompts not necessary

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Instruction fine-tuning has made it possible for Large Language Models (LLMs) to transfer to unseen tasks at scale. Because people want to use LLMs as versatile natural language processors, there is now an immediate effort to find out how well they do zero-shot on challenging tasks. Social media analysis is an active research area and it has a number of complex, domain-specific tasks, which can be used for harm reduction and for preventing the spread of misinformation. LLMs have a lot of potential to help with these computational social science (CSS) tasks, both for automatic data annotation and for social media analysis. So it is important to understand what the latest instruction fine-tuned LLMs can and cannot do on these CSS tasks. In this paper we mainly focus on answering the following research questions (RQ):

- (RQ 1) What zero-shot performance can LLMs get on social media classification tasks? How does this compare to smaller state-of-the-art language models that are fine-tuned on the specific task?

- (RQ 2) Which LLM prompt strategies work best for social media classification tasks in a zero-shot setting?

- (RQ 3) Did the pre-training corpus of the large model already include these datasets before the experiment (i.e., data leakage)?

- Setup
  - controlled experiments, two off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLMs, different prompting strategies
  - GPT-3.5-turbo (GPT): most widely used proprietary; OpenAssistant-LLaMA (LLaMA-OA): open source, based on LLaMA
  - six social media analysis NLP tasks, prompt complexity levels (few-shot examples, publication info of datasets)
  - baselines e.g. fine-tuning BERT
- Scope
  - off-the-shelf instruction-tuned models, zero-shot; foundation models without instruction tuning out of scope
- Findings
  - (i) task-specific fine-tuned models generally beat LLMs zero-shot, even much smaller ones (e.g. BERT-large)
  - (ii) prompting ensembles (e.g. on synonyms) help performance and robustness
  - (iii) detailed/complex prompts not necessary

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Instruction fine-tuning has made it possible for Large Language Models (LLMs) to transfer to unseen tasks at scale. Because people want to use LLMs as versatile natural language processors, there is now an immediate effort to find out how well they do zero-shot on challenging tasks. Social media analysis is an active research area and it has a number of complex, domain-specific tasks, which can be used for harm reduction and for preventing the spread of misinformation. LLMs have a lot of potential to help with these computational social science (CSS) tasks, both for automatic data annotation and for social media analysis. So it is important to understand what the latest instruction fine-tuned LLMs can and cannot do on these CSS tasks. In this paper we mainly focus on answering the following research questions (RQ):

- (RQ 1) What zero-shot performance can LLMs get on social media classification tasks? How does this compare to smaller state-of-the-art language models that are fine-tuned on the specific task?

- (RQ 2) Which LLM prompt strategies work best for social media classification tasks in a zero-shot setting?

- (RQ 3) Did the pre-training corpus of the large model already include these datasets before the experiment (i.e., data leakage)?

To answer these questions we run a series of controlled experiments where we look at the zero-shot performance of two off-the-shelf instruction fine-tuned large language models with different prompting strategies. The two models are GPT-3.5-turbo (GPT), which is the most widely used proprietary instruction fine-tuned large language model, and OpenAssistant-LLaMA (LLaMA-OA), which is an open source LLM that is instruction fine-tuned based on LLaMA. We use six social media analysis NLP tasks to evaluate how the LLMs do at classification with prompts of different complexity levels (including giving few-shot examples and the publication information of the benchmark datasets in the prompt). We also compare the results against baselines that use standard techniques, like fine-tuning BERT.

We should note that the scope of this paper is evaluating off-the-shelf, instruction fine-tuned language models on social media classification tasks, in a zero-shot setting. Evaluating foundation language models that are not instruction fine-tuned is out of scope here.

Our main findings are:

- (i) Models fine-tuned for the specific task still generally do better than LLMs in most zero-shot settings, even when the fully fine-tuned model (e.g., BERT-large) is a lot smaller.

- (ii) Prompting ensemble methods (e.g., on synonyms) can improve the performance and robustness of LLMs.

- (iii) Detailed and complex prompting strategies are not needed.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Instruction fine-tuning [1] has facilitated transfer learning for Large Language Models (LLMs) to unseen tasks at scale. To use LLMs as versatile natural language processors, there is an immediate effort to find out their zero-shot performance on challenging tasks. Social media analysis is an active area of research with a number of complex, domain-specific tasks which can be used for harm reduction [2] and preventing the spread of misinformation [3]. LLMs have great potential to assist with such computational social science (CSS) tasks, both in automatic data annotation and social media analysis [4,5,6]. Hence, it is important to understand the capabilities and limitations of the latest instruction fine-tuned LLMs for these CSS tasks. In this paper, we primarily focus on answering the following research questions (RQ):

- • (RQ 1) What level of zero-shot performance can LLMs achieve in social media classification tasks? How does zero-shot LLM performance compare against smaller state-of-the-art language models fine-tuned to the specific task?

- • (RQ 2) What are the most effective LLM prompt strategies for social media classification tasks in a zero-shot setting?

- • (RQ 3) Was the pre-training corpus of the large model already inclusive of these datasets before the experiment (i.e., data leakage issues)?

To answer these research questions, we conduct a series of controlled experiments investigating the zero-shot performance of two off-the-shelf instruction fine-tuned large language models with different prompting strategies. Namely, we experiment with GPT-3.5-turbo (GPT), the most widely used proprietary instruction fine-tuned large language model; and OpenAssistant-LLaMA (LLaMA-OA) [7], an open source LLM instruction fine-tuned based on LLaMA [8]. We use six social media analysis NLP tasks to evaluate the classification performance of LLMs with different levels of prompt complexity (including providing few-shot examples and publication information of the benchmark datasets in the prompt). The findings are also compared against baselines using standard techniques such as fine-tuning BERT.

It should be noted that the scope of this paper is evaluating the performance of off-the-shelf, instruction fine-tuned language models on social media classification tasks in a zero-shot setting. Evaluating foundation language models without instruction fine-tuning is out of the scope of this paper.

Our main findings are:

- • (i) Task-specific fine-tuned models still generally tend to outperform LLMs in most zero-shot settings, even when the fully fine-tuned model (e.g., BERT-large model) is much smaller.

- • (ii) Using prompting ensemble methods (e.g., on synonyms) can increase the performance and robustness of LLMs.

- • (iii) Detailed and complex prompting strategies are not necessary.
